subject: Art & Design
title: Accessibility: Inclusive Design Is Better Design
description: Learn Accessibility: Inclusive Design Is Better Design in one minute.

hook.text: 1 billion people worldwide have disabilities. If your design excludes them, you've just lost 15% of your audience.

buildup.text: Accessible design works for everyone: screen reader users, color-blind individuals, motor-impaired users, and more.

discovery.text: Curb cuts were designed for wheelchairs. Now everyone uses them: parents with strollers, cyclists, delivery workers.

twist.text: Accessibility improvements often benefit all users. High contrast helps in sunlight. Captions help in noisy cafés.

climax.text: Microsoft's inclusive design framework starts with 'permanent' disabilities and extends to temporary and situational.

punchline.text: Designing for the extremes improves the experience for the middle.

quiz.question: What does the curb cut effect demonstrate about accessible design?
options: Features designed for disabilities often benefit everyone
Only wheelchair users benefit from curb cuts
Accessibility features are expensive and rarely used

details.summary: Accessible design ensures products work for people with disabilities — visual impairments, motor limitations, cognitive differences, and hearing loss. Far from constraining creativity, accessible design produces cleaner interfaces, better contrast, clearer language.
details.whyItMatters: Over one billion people worldwide have disabilities. Accessible design isn't charity — it's good business, legal compliance, and fundamentally better design. Curb cuts, designed for wheelchairs, benefit everyone with strollers, luggage, and bicycles.
takeaways: Accessible design serves over one billion people with disabilities
Accessibility constraints produce better design for all users
Curb cut effect: disability accommodations benefit everyone

faq.question: What is the curb cut effect?
faq.answer: Curb cuts — ramps at sidewalk edges — were designed for wheelchair users but benefit everyone: parents with strollers, travelers with luggage, delivery workers with carts. Similarly, closed captions help people in noisy environments, high contrast helps users in bright sunlight.

faq.question: What are the most important accessibility guidelines?
faq.answer: Sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 minimum for text), keyboard navigability for all interactive elements, alt text for images, semantic HTML for screen readers, focus indicators for keyboard users, and no reliance on color alone to convey meaning.
